67.wh: Traditional methods either require many samples per material (expensive to measure and store) or use rigid mathematical models that don't capture real-world complexity. Modern measurements produce high-dimensional data (viewing angle, illumination angle, wavelength), and standard interpolation methods either bloat the representation or smooth away important fine structure like specular peaks and anisotropic patterns.
67.ap: This method uses Bayesian regression with a Gaussian process—a statistical framework that treats the material's reflectivity as a smooth function and learns it from sparse samples. Instead of the usual Gaussian kernel, it uses a generalized distance covariance kernel specifically designed to preserve fine features in material appearance (like sharp specular highlights). The data is organized cleverly so that factorization dramatically reduces the dimensionality, making the computation tractable—fitting and rendering both reduce to matrix operations.
67.ww: Gaussian processes provide a principled uncertainty estimate; they know which regions of the material's properties are well-constrained and which are not. The custom kernel respects the structure of material appearance better than generic smoothing. Factorization exploits the inherent separability in material data (viewing angle decouples from illumination angle in certain coordinate systems), avoiding the full curse of dimensionality.
67.po: A complete BRDF representation fits in seconds rather than hours or days, is compact enough for real-time rendering, and adapts its complexity to match the material's actual complexity. The representation converts easily to standard rendering formats, making it plug-and-play for existing graphics pipelines. Different materials—isotropic brushed metals, anisotropic fabrics, pearls—all work uniformly.

68.bp: Discrete X-ray tomography reconstructs what's inside an object—a cast iron engine block, an aluminum bracket, a composite material—by shooting X-rays through it at many angles and reconstructing the 3D composition from the 2D radiographs. When only a handful of angles are available (the practical, radiation-safe case), reconstruction becomes dramatically harder and ambiguous.
68.wh: With few images, many different internal structures could plausibly produce the same X-ray shadows. Standard tomography algorithms (SIRT, DART, TVR-DART) use handcrafted constraints and heuristics that work for simple cases but struggle with sparse or limited-angle data—they get stuck in local minima and produce artifacts. These methods also ignore subtle effects like X-rays scattering inside the object.
68.ap: This method treats the problem as inverse rendering: instead of simulating X-rays from a known object, it inverts the process. Each location in the 3D volume is represented as a probability distribution over the known materials (steel is likely here, air is likely there). The method minimizes a loss function by comparing predicted X-rays (computed by simulating rays through the probabilistic volume) to the measured X-rays. Gradients flow backward through the ray simulation, adjusting the material probabilities to fit the data better. It naturally incorporates scattering and works on GPUs.
68.ww: Gradient-based optimization is powerful and flexible—it can incorporate nonlinear effects like scattering that traditional methods ignore. The probabilistic formulation naturally handles uncertainty; regions with conflicting evidence become ambiguous (high entropy) rather than forced into one material. GPU parallelization makes the optimization tractable even with fine spatial resolution.
68.po: Reconstruction quality surpasses traditional methods, especially in sparse and limited-angle scenarios where ambiguity is highest. The method handles scattering and nonlinear effects that other approaches miss, and the probabilistic output tells you which reconstructed details are confident versus ambiguous—critical information for engineering decisions.

69.bp: Determining whether a point is inside or outside a 3D shape is a fundamental operation in computer graphics, simulation, and manufacturing. You need it to check if an object has collided with something, to apply volume forces, to slice shapes in CAD software, or to prepare geometry for 3D printing. The method must work on any shape—open surfaces, self-intersecting meshes, tangled or non-manifold geometry—that real data contains.
69.wh: Ray casting dominates the cost; the new formulation reduces it dramatically by exploiting the sphere projection structure. The boundary integral component handles tricky cases (tangent intersections, small loops) that raw ray casting misses. Precomputation and GPU implementation reach billions of queries per second.
69.ap: This method expresses insidedness as the sum of two geometric quantities: the signed number of times a ray pierces the surface, and a boundary integral computed over the surface's projection onto a sphere surrounding the query point. The integral is rewritten to avoid expensive surface calculations—it becomes a 2D computation on the sphere projection instead. For meshes, this discretizes efficiently. For curved parametric surfaces, the method adapts the same principle with analytic precision.
69.po: Speedups of 22× on CPU and 109 queries per second on GPU make generalized winding numbers practical for real-time geometry processing, large-scale simulations, and interactive design. The same algorithm works uniformly on meshes and smooth surfaces, open and closed, manifold and non-manifold—solving a long-standing robustness problem.

70.bp: Architects design beautiful freeform surfaces—curved facades, flowing shells, undulating roofs—but actually building them is expensive because you can't cut them from flat sheet materials efficiently. The solution is panelization: approximating the freeform surface with an assembly of flat polygonal panels that can be cut from wood, metal, or glass and then assembled. The panels must fit the surface tightly and also support their own weight and external loads (snow, wind) without deforming or breaking.
70.wh: Panelization is a two-way fight: make the panels very small and flat-fitting, but the structure becomes expensive and complex; make them larger and simpler, and the deviation from the intended shape becomes visible. The structural requirements are global—a weak spot creates cascading stress concentrations that might require reinforcement far away. Solving panelization and structural optimization separately usually yields compromises; jointly optimizing both is hard because you have many combinatorial choices (which boundary vertices form a panel?) coupled to complex nonlinear stress analysis.
70.ap: The method formulates panelization as continuous surface flow where candidate panels are creased elastic shells (like origami). Rather than choosing panel edges discretely, the algorithm flows the surface toward an optimal panelization while simultaneously computing internal stresses. The objective function integrates an arbitrary stress-based measure (minimize peak stress, or spread stress evenly) over the shell. Gradients of this objective with respect to the surface shape enable gradient-based optimization, and terms in the flow encourage the result to stay close to the original design intent.
70.ww: Continuous flow converts the discrete combinatorial problem into a smooth optimization, enabling gradient methods. Creased shells can be analyzed as simple elastic structures, making stress computation and differentiation tractable. The integrated objective couples geometry and mechanics throughout optimization, so the algorithm never settles on a geometrically beautiful but structurally weak solution.
70.po: Panelizations are geometrically faithful to the original freeform design and structurally optimized for fabrication loads—no post-hoc reinforcement needed. The method accelerates architectural fabrication workflows and enables more ambitious freeform designs to be built cost-effectively.

71.bp: Self-intersecting surfaces (where the surface pierces through itself) break downstream pipelines: physics simulations diverge, 3D printing fails, and machine learning models trained on valid geometry behave unexpectedly. Untangling surfaces—removing self-intersections while preserving the intended shape—is essential for cleaning up 3D scans, procedurally generated geometry, and artistic models.
71.wh: Self-intersections are global topological tangles, not local collisions; moving two vertices apart in one spot may create new intersections elsewhere. Local collision-response methods (push vertices away from each other) often just shift the problem. A true fix requires reasoning about the overall shape configuration simultaneously, which most methods don't do.
71.ap: This method defines two energies: a shape-level energy that penalizes global entanglement (measured in the continuous surface, independent of how finely it's tessellated), and a mesh-level energy that prevents local discrete interactions (triangles piercing through each other). Together, they enforce embeddedness—the geometric property that a surface doesn't self-intersect. The framework works on surfaces with boundary, non-manifold configurations, multi-object scenes, and handles cases where the surface has immersion failures (high curvature pathologies).
71.ww: The shape-level energy prevents the untangling from just shifting self-intersections rather than removing them; it's insensitive to mesh resolution, so coarse and fine meshes converge to the same shape. The mesh-level penalty catches local discrete issues that the shape-level energy might miss. Neither energy requires modifying the mesh connectivity, so the untangling respects the user's intended surface topology.
71.po: Complex self-tangled surfaces untangle reliably across varied geometry types and dataset challenges, enabling robust downstream processing. Scanned point clouds converted to mesh, procedurally generated shapes, and hand-sculpted models all now have a single, reliable untangling mechanism that preserves artistic intent while removing pathologies.

72.bp: Generating diverse, high-quality 3D shapes on demand—furniture, tools, characters, creatures—is valuable for design, gaming, and storytelling. Existing generative models (diffusion and autoregressive) produce excellent results but require many generation steps, making them slow. Faster inference enables interactive design and real-time applications.
72.wh: Standard diffusion and autoregressive models generate the entire shape incrementally, which requires dozens to hundreds of steps. Recent work shows that next-scale prediction—generating coarser structures first, then refining them level by level—is faster and higher quality, but this works only for fixed-resolution grids. Real 3D data is often sparse (most of space is empty), so fixed grids waste computation on empty regions. Adaptive variable-length representations like sparse octrees are more efficient but incompatible with existing next-scale methods.
72.ap: This method encodes 3D shapes into a multiscale octree representation using a specialized compression network (VQ-VAE with residual serialization). An octree is a hierarchical tree where each level subdivides space more finely—like a zoom-in-and-refine view. A generative model then predicts the octree structure and geometry features level by level, from coarse to fine. The key innovation is an attention mechanism that understands octree structure and only attends to truly relevant features at each scale, avoiding wasted computation on empty or irrelevant branches.
72.ww: Octrees naturally compress sparse shapes, eliminating the resolution waste of fixed grids. Next-scale prediction is fast because each level is a small prediction task; coarse levels guide subsequent refinements. Octree-aware attention focuses computation where it matters, respecting the hierarchical structure rather than treating space uniformly.
72.po: High-quality 3D shapes generate in a small number of steps, orders of magnitude faster than standard diffusion or autoregressive models. This enables interactive shape creation, real-time game asset generation, and design workflows where artists iterate rapidly.

73.bp: NURBS surfaces (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) are the standard mathematical representation for curves and surfaces in CAD systems and design software. When two NURBS surfaces meet, their intersection curve defines edges and seams in the model. Computing this intersection correctly is fundamental to CAD reliability; mistakes in topology (failing to detect a loop, missing an isolated point) cause cascading failures in downstream operations.
73.wh: Identifying all intersection branches robustly is hard because complex topology can include tiny loops (nearly tangent curves that form small loops before separating), degenerate tangent intersections (curves touching but not crossing), and self-intersections. Industrial methods work most of the time but fail on edge cases. Existing approaches trade speed for robustness; catching all topology is slow.
73.ap: The method detects intersection branches by computing their starting points robustly. It combines winding number theory (a mathematical tool for counting how many times a curve winds around a point) with a subdivision scheme. The idea is to find points on the parametric domain where the vector field (a mathematical representation of potential intersection directions) has special structure (singularities). Winding numbers detect small loops and isolated singularities; subdivision localizes tangent intersection points precisely.
73.ww: Winding numbers count global topology without explicitly computing intersections, making small loops visible even if they're nearly tangent. Subdivision converges to tangent points precisely. Starting points are more robust to compute than full curves, so the method avoids numerical creep and instability that plague direct curve tracing.
73.po: Topologically correct intersection computation on complex inputs—small loops, tangencies, degenerate configurations—now outperforms both commercial and open-source CAD kernels. This improves reliability of CAD systems for manufacturing, design fabrication, and complex assemblies where topological errors are expensive.

74.bp: Knitted garments—sweaters, socks, scarves—have richly detailed structure: yarn strands interlock in complex patterns. Simulating knitwear at the yarn level (rather than treating it as a triangular mesh) captures intricate wrinkles, folds, and draping that matter for visual realism in high-end animation. However, yarn-level simulation is computationally prohibitive; each stitch involves thousands of tiny degrees of freedom.
74.wh: Yarn-level knitwear has multiple competing physical effects: stretching and compression in the yarn, bending resistance (yarn doesn't fold like paper), twisting, shearing, and contacts where yarns collide. These effects are tightly coupled and nonlinear, making optimization per frame slow. Standard numerical methods require expensive line searches and frequent small steps because the system is non-convex (multiple local solutions exist).
74.ap: The method extends Douglas-Rachford Splitting (DRS), an optimization algorithm, to handle non-convex problems. The key innovation is nested decomposition: instead of solving the full coupled problem, it breaks it into independent sub-problems (one for stretching, one for bending, etc.), each of which is convex (has a single optimum). The nested structure ensures these sub-problems couple correctly across yarn threads and contacts. The paper derives principled metric selection for each sub-problem based on convergence theory, replacing ad-hoc tuning.
74.ww: Splitting converts a hard non-convex problem into a sequence of easier convex sub-problems, improving robustness and convergence. Convexity eliminates the need for line searches and frequent convergence checks. Theoretical metric selection grounds parameter choices, yielding near-optimal convergence without trial-and-error.
74.po: Yarn-level knitwear simulates efficiently enough for animation workflows, maintaining high-resolution detail and realistic deformation without the computational burden that previously limited adoption. This enables feature-quality cloth simulation with yarn-level realism in film and animation pipelines.

75.bp: Telescopes and microscopes struggle to see clearly through turbulent air or cloudy glass — the atmosphere or optical imperfections scramble incoming light waves. We want to correct this distortion in real-time and in software, recovering sharp images of distant objects without needing artificial reference beacons (guidestars) placed in the sky.
75.wh: Measuring how much the light has been distorted requires knowing either the original light pattern (which you don't have for natural scenes) or a bright reference star at a known position (which may not exist or be too faint). The trick is getting the wavefront measurement from the blurry image alone, using only the quirky shape of the telescope's opening.
75.ap: They use an asymmetric telescope pupil (an oddly-shaped opening instead of a circular one) that encodes wavefront distortions into measurable patterns in the image. Two neural networks then infer the optical distortion from these patterns and predict what the true image looks like. A deformable mirror at the pupil plane applies the computed correction optically, closing the loop in real-time.
75.ww: An asymmetric pupil breaks the symmetry of how light spreads in the image, so the blurry pattern itself now contains information about the distortion — like a broken mirror shape tells you how light was bent. Neural networks learn this relationship from training data, so correcting distortions that haven't been seen before still works reasonably well.
75.po: The system corrects optical aberrations without a guidestar, uses 100× fewer images, and needs 1000× less computation than older phase-retrieval methods. It enables sharp imaging of natural scenes through unknown obstacles (dust, haze, or fog) with only a camera and a controllable mirror.

76.bp: Quad meshes are four-sided grids that artists and engineers drape over 3D shapes to control how surfaces behave and look — they're essential for character animation, manufacturing, and numerical simulation. Hand-drawing these grids is tedious and requires expertise, so automating the process would save enormous time.
76.wh: Neural networks that directly predict quad grids struggle because small changes in the shape create large, chaotic shifts in the quad pattern, even when the underlying 'singularities' (special points where quads meet at odd angles) barely move. This creates visually jarring, inconsistent results when you blend multiple suggestions.
76.ap: Instead of predicting the entire quad grid, they train a network to predict only the sparse singular points: where they lie and their 'index' (how many quads spiral around them). They convert this into auxiliary fields to make the learning problem well-behaved. Then conventional algorithms smoothly connect the singular points to build the full, coherent quad grid.
76.ww: Singular points are the core structure that determines a quad grid's shape. By learning those rare, stable points instead of the millions of quad edges, the network sees a cleaner problem with less noise. The subsequent smooth-connection step (done non-neuronally) guarantees that the final grid is always valid and coherent, regardless of small prediction errors.
76.po: The method generates smooth, topologically varying quad grids and simplifies dataset preparation. Results are stable across shape variations and automatically handle coordinate invariance and insensitivity to tessellation choices — properties that matter for production automation.

77.bp: Relit portrait videos are videos where the lighting on an actor's face is changed after filming — perhaps to match a new scene or mood. The challenge is making the relighting look photorealistic and keeping it consistent frame-to-frame so the actor's face doesn't flicker or look artificial.
77.wh: Older methods either work on still images (ignoring flicker) or are too slow for video. Building a learning model requires diverse training data showing the same actor under many different lighting conditions, which is expensive to capture. Generative models also struggle to preserve fine facial details (skin tone, wrinkles, hair) while changing lighting.
77.ap: They built a physical LED lighting rig to capture real portrait videos under known lighting. A diffusion model (a generative tool that learns patterns by removing noise from images) is trained on this hybrid dataset of real and rendered videos. At runtime, the model takes an HDR environment map (a 360-degree image describing the new lighting) and synthesizes the relit frame.
77.ww: Diffusion models are naturally good at preserving details (like wrinkles) while smoothing unrealistic lighting artifacts because they learn what real skin looks like under varied light. The real LED captures and the HDR control signal together teach the model to respect both identity and photorealism. Temporal consistency emerges because the underlying video diffusion model is trained to keep motion smooth.
77.po: Videos relight with photorealistic quality, preserve the actor's expression and fine facial features, and generalize to unseen subjects, motions, and new lighting conditions. The model works on in-the-wild videos (filmed normally) with no manual setup.

78.bp: In virtual reality, the delay between when you move your head and when the display updates (latency) makes you feel disconnected and dizzy. Lower latency makes VR feel more real and responsive. Current headsets have 12-60 ms latency; understanding whether even lower latencies matter for user comfort and performance requires a device that can test it.
78.wh: Modern VR systems use clever tricks (pose prediction, late reprojection) to hide latency, but these tricks only work down to about 12 ms. Testing true latencies below that requires new hardware that doesn't need those tricks — a much harder engineering problem.
78.ap: They built a video passthrough headset called Camsicle with two cameras and a special mirror-lens system (catadioptric design) that displays the real world with only 2 milliseconds of end-to-end latency. The cameras capture what you see, the system processes it instantly, and the display shows it with virtually no delay.
78.ww: By using cameras and mirrors instead of prediction hacks, there's no accumulated error — the user sees the physical world nearly as if the headset weren't there. This true low-latency passthrough is the key to testing whether sub-12-ms latencies actually matter for user preference, rather than just theory.
78.po: User studies with 57 participants show that 2 ms and 14.3 ms latencies are preferred over 23 and 29 ms in a ball-catching task. The platform enables perceptual research on latency thresholds that was previously impossible, grounding subjective VR comfort in measurable physical quantities.

79.bp: When fungi decay wood, they don't just eat away randomly — they break down specific chemicals (lignin, sugars, defenses), and the wood's moisture and grain structure determine how fast and where the decay spreads and causes structural failure. Simulating this process realistically would help visualize how trees rot and inform timber engineering.
79.wh: Wood decay couples biology (fungal spread, chemical degradation), fluid flow (moisture moving through grain), and mechanics (wood fracturing and hollowing) in complex ways. Each domain has different physics, and they strongly influence each other. No prior method unified them.
79.ap: They represent wood as a 3D volumetric model with explicit grain alignment, internal moisture, and tissue health states (intact, colonized, consumed). They simulate three coupled processes: anisotropic spread of fungal colonies (following grain and moisture), consumption of wood resources, and stress-driven fracture patterns (driven by moisture and material loss).
79.ww: Tracking moisture, fungal spread, and material failure together lets each influence the others correctly. Fungal spread follows grain (anisotropic), so it doesn't just make a sphere around the infection point. Moisture and chemical consumption weaken wood locally, leading to realistic cuboid fracture patterns (characteristic of rot) rather than smooth erosion.
79.po: Simulations realistically capture the progression of rot: fungal colonization spread, characteristic cube-shaped fracture patterns, trunk hollowing, and environmental moisture effects on structural stability. The rendering shows volumetric decay as a realistic 3D process, not an abstract animation.

80.bp: When you scan a 3D shape with sensors (cameras, LiDAR) or reconstruct it from partial data, there's always uncertainty — ambiguity about the exact surface. Most geometry processing assumes a single, definite shape, throwing away that uncertainty. The goal is to do useful operations (smoothing, curvature, flow) while acknowledging and using the uncertainty.
80.wh: Classical geometry processing (computing gradients, Laplacians, running smoothing algorithms) assumes a crisp, deterministic surface. But if the input is uncertain, a single fixed surface can mask important ambiguities. Building math for uncertain surfaces from scratch is non-trivial.
80.ap: They use Gaussian Process Implicit Surfaces, a probabilistic representation that stores a distribution over plausible shapes instead of one fixed shape. They define analogs of classical operators (gradient, divergence, Laplacian) that work on this distribution, computing expected values using the Kac-Rice formula (a tool from random surface theory).
80.ww: Gaussian processes naturally encode uncertainty, and the Kac-Rice formula lets you compute integrals and derivatives over random surfaces by embedding them into a fixed volumetric domain. This converts an intractable problem (differentiate a probabilistic surface) into an integral over a volume, which is computationally tractable.
80.po: You can now do geometry processing (like smoothing or curvature estimation) that accounts for input noise and ambiguity rather than pretending the input is perfect. This bridges classical surface equations and modern probabilistic shape representations, enabling principled handling of noisy or incomplete scans.

81.bp: In video games, movies, and robotics, characters need to move in real-time with precise control — walk faster, face a direction, reach for an object. Generative AI can synthesize convincing motions, but it's slow and hard to control in the fine-grained, multi-faceted way that production pipelines need.
81.wh: Generative models trained on massive motion datasets can produce diverse and realistic motion, but they require seconds of computation. Real-time demands milliseconds. Existing models also respond poorly to multi-modal control: velocity commands, style choices, and exact keyframes simultaneously, which production rarely addresses.
81.ap: MotionBricks uses a large modular neural backbone trained on 350,000 motion clips that generates motions in a learned 'latent' space (compressed, efficient representation). On top, 'smart primitives' provide an authoring interface for intuitive control: speed commands, style labels, and spatial keyframe constraints. The model learns to blend these controls naturally.
81.ww: Modularity means the core model learns general motion patterns once, then different downstream tasks (walking, reaching, dancing) reuse the same backbone without retraining. Smart primitives encode common control needs so the system learns what users actually want without task-specific annotations. This amortizes computation across many use cases.
81.po: The system generates diverse motions in real-time (critical for interactive apps), supports multi-modal control (velocity, style, keyframes), and works on new tasks zero-shot (without fine-tuning). It bridges the gap between research generative methods and production demands for control and speed.

82.bp: Teaching robots to move like humans is hard: human motions evolved for human bodies, but robots have different arm lengths, joint ranges, and physics. Naively copying a human motion onto a quadruped or unusual robot often produces sliding feet, self-collisions, or motions that violate physics, so the robot can't actually execute them.
82.wh: Retargeting (adapting a reference motion to a new body) is traditionally done by hand or with heuristics that ignore physics. If you account for physics, the optimization becomes complex and brittle. Reinforcement learning can produce physically valid motions, but it requires a lot of trial-and-error.
82.ap: ReActor uses a two-level optimization: the top level adapts the reference motion's parameters (e.g., joint angles) to match the robot's shape, and the bottom level trains a tracking policy using reinforcement learning to follow the adapted motion while respecting physics constraints. They derive approximations to make the bilevel problem solvable.
82.ww: By tightly coupling retargeting and RL training, the motion adapts to the specific robot body and the physics constraints, rather than one then the other. RL ensures the final motion is actually feasible for the robot to execute. The framework needs only sparse semantic hints (which human joints map to which robot joints), not manual tuning.
82.po: Robots can execute retargeted motions without foot sliding, self-collision, or dynamic infeasibility, even when retargeting to very different morphologies (e.g., a quadruped from a human). The method validates on real hardware, making human-inspired motion practical for robotics.

83.bp: Rendering complex 3D volumes (smoke, clouds, semi-transparent materials) is computationally expensive. To speed it up, we use hierarchies: show low detail far from the camera and high detail up close. This is easy with traditional voxel grids but hard with modern Gaussian-based representations, which are memory-efficient but don't have built-in levels of detail.
83.wh: Gaussian representations avoid the memory cost of voxel grids, but constructing a hierarchical version is awkward: prefiltering bloats memory, recomputing each level is expensive, and smooth transitions between levels are hard to guarantee. You need a method that prunes or filters without refitting.
83.ap: Gabor Fields replace Gaussian elements with Gabor kernels (sinusoidal functions modulated by a Gaussian envelope) that naturally encode frequency and orientation. Rendering can select which frequencies to use at each viewing distance. Pruning high-frequency kernels automatically reduces detail without refitting or extra storage.
83.ww: Gabor kernels inherently encode frequency information (spatial scale), so reducing detail is as simple as dropping the high-frequency components. This is cheap and automatic, unlike Gaussian prefiltering. Stochastically sampling different frequencies at different ray depths creates smooth transitions between hierarchy levels.
83.po: Gabor Fields enable smooth, continuous level-of-detail for Gaussian volumes with no refitting, no extra memory, and faster rendering. Ray traversal accelerates because high-frequency components can be masked, allowing the renderer to skip large volumetric regions.

84.bp: Heat transfer in 3D shapes with realistic radiation (where hot surfaces emit infrared and cool other surfaces) is governed by complex equations that require numerical solving. Thermal simulations matter for engineering and also for graphics (hot metal rendering). Monte Carlo methods handle complex geometry robustly, but they don't yet handle the nonlinear radiation boundary conditions.
84.wh: Radiation produces a nonlinear boundary condition (the heat loss depends on the surface temperature to the fourth power, following Stefan-Boltzmann law). Nonlinear equations are much harder to solve than linear ones. Existing Monte Carlo PDE solvers handle linear boundary conditions but not this nonlinearity.
84.ap: They use Picard fixed-point iteration: repeatedly update boundary conditions and resolve the PDE, letting the solution converge by successive approximations. A denoising technique using heteroscedastic regression reduces the variance of Monte Carlo estimates at boundaries, focusing effort where it matters most.
84.ww: Picard iteration converts a hard nonlinear problem into a sequence of easier linear solves. Each solve uses Monte Carlo's robustness on complex geometry. The denoising step targets boundary variance specifically, filling a gap that prior methods (which denoised only interior points) left open.
84.po: Monte Carlo solvers now handle nonlinear thermal radiation boundaries with significantly higher accuracy than linearization approximations. The method works on complex geometries (the whole point of Monte Carlo) and is empirically stable even with bad initial guesses.

85.bp: Animating 3D human characters in real-time for interactive games or VR requires generating believable motion fast and with responsive control — the player says "walk forward and turn left" and the character does it immediately, in a natural way, matching the narrative voice they requested.
85.wh: Offline generative models produce high-quality motion but are too slow for interactivity. Online methods are fast but often lack nuanced control (text semantics, long-horizon goals) and struggle to maintain temporal coherence over long sequences. The two worlds haven't converged.
85.ap: ARDY (Autoregressive Diffusion) streams motion generation in real-time using a hybrid representation: the character's root position (where they're walking) is explicit for precise control, and the body's pose is learned in a latent space for efficiency. A two-stage transformer-denoiser with variable context window generates new poses conditioned on text prompts and keyframe constraints.
85.ww: The hybrid representation separates concerns: trajectory control (where the character walks) is direct and stable, while body animation (posture, arm swing) is learned flexibly. Variable context lets the model look at different amounts of past motion depending on the situation. Training on text labels and ground-truth keyframes teaches the model to fuse both signals naturally.
85.po: The system generates high-fidelity human motion in real-time, responsive to text prompts and flexible kinematic constraints, with support for long-horizon goals. It bridges offline quality and online speed, enabling interactive animation with semantic and spatial control that was previously unavailable.

86.bp: Winding numbers answer a fundamental question: is a point inside or outside a 3D shape? This seems simple for clean, closed surfaces, but real meshes are messy — they have gaps, overlaps, and curved boundaries. A robust inside-outside test is essential for simulation, texturing, and boolean operations.
86.wh: Direct evaluation of winding numbers on large, complex meshes is slow, so spatial acceleration is needed. Existing fast methods approximate by clustering primitives far from the query point. But they only work on discrete meshes (triangles, points), not smooth curves or patches.
86.ap: They extend winding number acceleration to curved geometry (NURBS curves and trimmed patches) using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy that stores precomputed moment data at each node. Queries use fast approximations for far clusters but directly evaluate nearby curved primitives, preserving geometric accuracy.
86.ww: Precomputing moments (integrals of basis functions) at hierarchy nodes enables accurate approximations for distant clusters without refitting. Direct evaluation near the query preserves fine details (like thin features) that would be lost with purely approximate methods. The two-tier strategy keeps asymptotic complexity low while maintaining accuracy.
86.po: Winding number queries on curved geometry (NURBS) achieve sub-linear complexity while preserving geometric features, enabling containment queries on arbitrary curved shapes — not just triangle meshes. This is useful for procedural design and simulation on parametric surfaces.

87.bp: Walk on Spheres (WoS) is a flexible, meshless method for solving partial differential equations (heat, diffusion) by simulating random walks. It's robust to complex geometry, but converges slowly, requiring millions of walks. The goal is to reuse information from intermediate points along walks to speed convergence.
87.wh: Each random walk in WoS visits many points before reaching a boundary, but classical methods discard all intermediate values and only record the final result. Using intermediate points seems promising, but their probability distribution (shaped by dynamically generated spheres) is intractable to evaluate.
87.ap: Walk on Probes (WoP) replaces dynamic spheres with fixed, pre-distributed probe spheres throughout the domain. This converts the tricky distribution of walk points into simple samples on fixed sphere boundaries. A Poisson integral formula then cheaply evaluates each intermediate point's contribution without needing to recompute from scratch.
87.ww: Fixed probe boundaries have known, tractable distributions (uniform on a sphere), so their contribution to the solution is easy to compute. By reusing intermediate points, each random walk becomes multiple independent unbiased estimates instead of just one, dramatically improving variance without additional simulations.
87.po: Walk on Probes substantially improves sample efficiency and convergence speed while preserving WoS's flexibility for complex geometries. The method is general: it combines reuse with control variates and self-normalization for further variance reduction.

88.bp: Winding numbers — a measure of whether a point is inside a 3D shape — are used constantly in graphics and simulation. Computing them naively on large meshes is slow, but existing fast methods use approximations. The goal is to compute exact winding numbers quickly on realistic, messy meshes with gaps and overlaps.
88.wh: The classical formula for winding numbers is a surface integral that's expensive to evaluate. Fast approximations lose accuracy on imperfect meshes. There's a tension between accuracy and speed that existing methods don't fully resolve.
88.ap: They analytically simplify the surface integral to just a single ray-mesh intersection test plus an elementary sum over boundary edges. This reduction is mathematically exact (no approximation), yet vastly faster than the direct integral because it replaces billions of floating-point operations with a few geometric queries.
88.ww: The mathematical reduction works because the integral has special structure: most of it cancels, leaving only the contribution from ray intersections and edges. By computing analytically what would be expensive numerically, they keep the algorithm exact while making it practical on large meshes.
88.po: Winding number queries are orders of magnitude faster than prior methods while remaining exact (only floating-point rounding error). The algorithm is simple, debuggable, and robust even on extremely noisy or corrupt meshes, making it a practical replacement for existing approximation methods.

89.bp: Fabric looks different under different lighting because of its fiber structure — how threads braid and bend affects how light bounces. Rendering fabric photorealistically requires capturing this structure at the fiber level, but current capture methods use expensive devices or hand-crafted pipelines. The goal is to infer fiber geometry and appearance from a single cheap microscope image.
89.wh: A microscope image and a final rendered image of woven fabric look vastly different — one is a 2D close-up of surface texture, the other a 3D view of complex shading. Inferring full 3D fiber geometry and optical properties from such minimal, 2D information seems under-constrained.
89.ap: They use differentiable procedural models: 3D fiber geometry and shading behavior are parameterized by a few numbers (thread thickness, weave pattern, fiber properties). A neural network predicts initial parameters, then optimization adjusts them to match the microscope image via differentiable rasterization (simulation-based fitting). Refinement improves details.
89.ww: Procedural models are expressive enough to capture real woven fabric but compact enough that optimization over parameters is tractable. Differentiable rasterization lets gradient-based optimization refine parameters to match observations. The coarse-to-fine approach first gets the macro structure right, then refines.
89.po: From a single microscope image, the method recovers fiber-level geometry and appearance suitable for photorealistic rendering. It sidesteps expensive CT scanners and manual authoring, enabling fiber-level fabric assets to be created from affordable tools.

90.bp: When you describe a shape as a mathematical function, you can render it anywhere with perfect precision. But those functions run slow on computers, especially inside graphics engines where we need to evaluate them billions of times per second. We want the speed of simple tricks with the precision of mathematics.
90.wh: The key insight is that implicit representations naturally become harder to get right as you move away from surfaces, and as local geometry gets more complex. A flat floor is easy; a sharp corner or thin feature is hard. But conventional models treat all locations identically.
90.ap: SAND learns a volumetric map recording how deep a network needs to go in each region to be accurate enough. It then uses a modified network architecture where layers can terminate early: each hidden layer has an output option (called a 'tail'), so computation can stop as soon as the necessary accuracy is reached, without traversing the entire network.
90.ww: This works because neural networks can learn internal shortcuts. If a region needs less accuracy, the network can produce good-enough answers partway through. By explicitly allowing early termination and learning where to terminate, the method directs computation only to places where it matters geometrically.
90.po: According to the abstract, SAND achieves spatial adaptivity without retraining—directing computational resources to geometrically important and complex regions. The result is faster sampling of shapes encoded as neural functions, making them practical for real-time graphics.

91.bp: 3D printers using molten plastic (FFF) can tilt their nozzle in any direction, not just print flat layers. This opens the door to printing without the stepped staircases that plague vertical walls and to using far less support material. But making this work requires solving intricate geometry problems that didn't exist in flat-layer printing.
91.wh: Tilting the nozzle means each layer is no longer flat. Layers must follow prescribed direction fields (user intent), keep constant bead thickness (the plastic comes out at a fixed rate), avoid collisions and tool retractions, and flow continuously from one layer to the next. Doing all of this simultaneously is combinatorially hard—every constraint couples to every other one.
91.ap: AtomSlicer encodes the shape using three perpendicular phase fields (a mathematical trick for describing geometry smoothly), samples them into oriented atoms (spatial building blocks), partitions the model into layers, reconstructs each layer as a mesh, and then synthesizes toolpaths aligned to user-specified direction fields. The key is treating those fields as hard constraints: if the geometry cannot be printed respecting the specification, the algorithm reports it rather than quietly breaking the rules.
91.ww: By separating the problem into phases—encoding, partitioning, reconstruction—the method avoids the combinatorial explosion of trying to optimize everything at once. Each phase works locally on clean geometric building blocks (atoms), so constraints decouple and become tractable.
91.po: The abstract shows AtomSlicer reduces non-extruding travel (wasted motion) to just a few percent and cuts travel moves by one to two orders of magnitude versus earlier methods. For a large test set of 10,000 shapes and 13 physical prints, it stays 9 to 60 times faster than competing algorithms.

92.bp: Imagine designing a living room: you mentally sketch the room's layout, picture where furniture fits, ensure nothing overlaps, and respect walls and doors. Creating realistic virtual rooms automatically is the same task, but machines must learn it. Today's methods either ignore spatial logic or drown in redundant connections, making them brittle and data-hungry.
92.wh: Scene design is a cascade of decisions. First, how many sofas and chairs? Then, how big? Then, where in the room and what spacing? Every decision depends on earlier ones, but also on the room's structure. A fully connected dependency graph between all objects creates redundancy and noise. Data scarcity makes learning hard.
92.ap: CasLayout breaks the problem into four discrete stages, each with explicit purpose: predict object counts and types, refine sizes and features, model spatial relations in a learned space (not pixel space), and generate precise bounding boxes. For spatial relations, the method builds a sparse graph (only relevant connections) rather than forcing every object to know about every other one. LLMs and vision-language models can guide the pipeline for zero-shot tasks like creating a scene from a photo.
92.ww: Breaking the task into stages mirrors how humans design: we sketch a plan, refine dimensions, check how objects relate, then finalize placement. Each stage focuses on one type of decision, so the network learns cleaner patterns. Sparse relations mean the model only learns necessary connections, not noise from irrelevant object pairs.
92.po: By decomposing the joint generation task, CasLayout reduces data requirements, maintains physical validity within floor plans by treating walls and doors as explicit constraints, and enables flexible integration with large language models for image-to-scene and text-to-scene generation.

93.bp: Matching points on two shapes—finding which part of the first surface corresponds to which part of the second—is central to animation, shape transfer, and reconstruction. The ideal match is bijective (one-to-one and reversible) and covers the whole surface without tearing. Finding such matches is notoriously hard.
93.wh: Existing algorithms rely on combinatorial operations (mesh connectivity changes), barrier functions that prevent overlap, or require a good initial guess. All of these are fragile: they fail on noisy data, require hand-tuning, and sometimes need manual setup. The problem is that bijectivity is a global topological property that resists local optimization.
93.ap: This paper represents the match as a 4-dimensional surface sitting in the product space formed by combining the two input surfaces. The map between the surfaces is stored implicitly—as the zero-set of a complex function (roughly, points where a complex number equals zero). Distortion is minimized by shrinking this mapping surface's area using the Ginzburg-Landau functional, a principle borrowed from physics and differential geometry that naturally favors smooth, minimal solutions.
93.ww: The Ginzburg-Landau functional, well-understood in physics, tends to prefer configurations that are globally optimal and smooth. By encoding bijectivity as an implicit geometric object and minimizing its area rather than penalizing overlap locally, the method sidesteps combinatorics. The implicit representation avoids mesh topology changes; the map is always continuous.
93.po: The result avoids combinatorial mesh modifications and barrier functions, making it more robust to noise and simpler to implement. It does not assume a good starting point and can untangle wrong matches from faster, cheaper methods. Landmark points or curves guide the optimization, giving designers control.

94.bp: In animation and engineering, we simulate how materials deform and flow—cloth, clay, snow, metals. Some materials are easy to simulate (soft and squishy), others are brutally hard (stiff rubber, plastic that resists deformation). Stiff materials demand tiny time steps, making simulations slow. We need stable, fast algorithms that handle the widest range of materials.
94.wh: Explicit time-stepping (the usual approach) requires tiny steps for stiff materials to remain stable—a CFL rate constraint. Implicit methods can use larger steps but create complex nonlinear systems that are expensive to solve. Standard implicit solvers also struggle when materials become nearly incompressible (volume-preserving).
94.ap: This method extends a mixed formulation (separating constraints from variables cleverly) to handle finite-strain viscoelasticity and general flow rules. The implicit time-stepping produces a symmetric optimization problem with compact stencils (local, sparse structure). The authors propose an efficient GPU solver, making the implicit system practical on modern hardware.
94.ww: By reformulating the equations as a symmetric optimization problem rather than a general nonlinear system, the solver can use better algorithms (like preconditioned conjugate gradient). Compact stencils mean sparse matrices and fast linear algebra. Running on GPUs adds massive parallelism.
94.po: The method enables stable simulation of stiff elastoviscoplastic materials up to the incompressible limit without requiring prohibitively small time steps. Examples range from granular materials and snow to elastic solids, and it supports two-way coupling with rigid bodies, greatly expanding the range of real-world phenomena that graphics pipelines can handle.

95.bp: Knowing what material an object is made of—its chemical composition or reflectance properties—requires measuring not just brightness but the full spectrum of light. Today's hyperspectral cameras are bulky and slow. We want spectrum measurement fast, in video, with passive indoor lighting, using tiny sensor chips.
95.wh: Single-photon sensors (SPAD) count individual light particles, giving extreme sensitivity and speed. But they produce quantized, nonlinear measurements with massive noise. Hyperspectral imaging normally requires many wavelength measurements per pixel. Combining both seems impossible: quantization and nonlinearity fight against spectral reconstruction.
95.ap: Hi-SPAD uses a pushbroom camera design (a line of pixels that sweeps across the scene) paired with SPAD sensors arranged in a grid that captures color. The system measures how many photons arrive in each tiny time window for each color band. Despite the heavy quantization and noise, reconstruction algorithms and material classification work by leveraging the fact that errors decrease exponentially as measurements accumulate.
95.ww: The key insight is that photon counting, while noisy per sample, improves steadily as you collect more measurements. With enough observations in the right setup (pushbroom plus color-sorted photon detectors), the nonlinearity becomes manageable. Theoretical analysis shows error bounds shrink exponentially, so practical reconstruction becomes feasible.
95.po: The lab-built Hi-SPAD camera achieves hyperspectral video at 26 frames per second with 123 spectral channels under ambient lighting. The abstract validates accurate material classification and full-spectrum reconstruction through simulation and real prototypes, establishing the feasibility of photon-counting hyperspectral video in dynamic scenes.

96.bp: The medial axis of a shape is its skeleton—the locus of centers of circles that touch the boundary from inside. It completely describes the original shape and is invaluable for shape analysis and animation. Computing a clean, accurate medial axis from a triangle mesh is notoriously hard; results are usually tangled and unstable.
96.wh: Without explicit correspondence between medial axis vertices and surface regions, the simplification process can destroy structural integrity. The medial axis may no longer faithfully capture the shape's geometry, especially near fillets and feature regions where the rolling-ball interpretation breaks down.
96.ap: Structural MAT tracks correspondence explicitly throughout simplification. Every medial axis vertex is labeled with the surface region(s) it corresponds to. Edge collapses are sequenced according to priority rules that respect this correspondence, ensuring medial axis triangles reflect true symmetries. The method treats correspondence as a geometric constraint governing the order of operations.
96.ww: By maintaining explicit correspondence, each medial axis feature remains tied to the surface symmetry it represents. Priority control ensures that important structural features (e.g., fillets) are preserved before simplifying less important parts. Correspondence also guides decisions about which edges should collapse, naturally enforcing boundary regularity.
96.po: The result is a medial axis that is runtime-efficient, structurally aligned with input geometry, has clean boundaries, high-quality triangles, and robust to noise. Performance improves across a large test set and on 10,000 diverse shapes; the method remains expressive for both articulated shapes and CAD models.

97.bp: Virtual reality feels immersive when you can touch and feel objects. Active haptic devices (motors, cables) that push back on your hands are ideal but bulky and expensive. The clever idea: use whatever's lying around in your room—a pillow, cup, table—as a stand-in for the virtual object you're touching.
97.wh: Finding the right physical proxy for a virtual object requires reasoning about both the virtual thing (how it should feel and resist touch) and the real environment (what objects are available, their material properties, their shape). A designer must annotate virtual objects with haptic hints, and the system must match those hints to real objects. This is inherently multimodal and ambiguous.
97.ap: ProXeek uses a large language model capable of vision and reasoning to solve this matching problem. Designers annotate virtual interactables with haptic characteristics via a node-based editor. When a user starts VR, they photograph their room using the VR headset. The LLM-based system combines understanding of the virtual haptics, the room's physical objects, and geometric constraints to find the best match.
97.ww: Large language models trained on diverse internet text and images have strong reasoning about objects, materials, and spatial fit. By framing the matching as a reasoning task (rather than pure geometry), the system can leverage semantic understanding: a squishy pillow "feels like" a cushioned seat; a wooden table is rigid. Multi-objective optimization balances multiple goals—comfort, realism, safety.
97.po: ProXeek effectively identifies viable proxies and delivers significantly higher haptic fidelity than 3D-printed replicas and visual-only interaction, according to user studies. It enables designers to opportunistically use real-world objects without pre-fabrication or special setup, making haptic VR practical in ordinary homes.

98.bp: Designing surfaces by hand is tedious—you move control points, waiting for the surface to update each time. Real-time deformation, where dragging a handle smoothly deforms the surface instantly, is what you want. Neural networks can fit surfaces to data beautifully, but they're black boxes that resist direct manipulation.
98.wh: Neural parametric surfaces fit detail well but break key geometric properties. Moving a control point should move only nearby surface—local control—and shouldn't break smoothness or require retraining. Neural networks globally couple all parameters to all outputs, so local intuitive edits are impossible.
98.ap: NeuBase pairs a traditional subdivision surface base (which has local control and smoothness built in) with an offset field defined by neural basis functions. The neural basis functions are encoded via a learned map. This hybrid approach lets the surface fit detail via neural learning while preserving the desirable properties of classical subdivision surfaces.
98.ww: By construction, the method maintains linearity (the surface depends linearly on control weights), locality (each control point influences only nearby surface), smoothness (inherited from subdivision), and affine equivariance (rotating the control mesh rotates the surface). These properties are not learned; they're architectural. So direct manipulation works without retraining.
98.po: NeuBase supports intuitive real-time surface deformation: designers deform the control mesh and see results instantly. The surface achieves better fitting accuracy than other neural parametric representations while staying efficient even for complex shapes with dense control meshes. It balances neural expressiveness with classical geometric guarantees.

99.bp: Many phenomena in graphics and engineering are governed by elliptic PDEs—Poisson's equation for smoke, heat transfer for materials, electromagnetic potentials. Solving them on complex evolving shapes (like deforming cloth or fracturing materials) is slow and requires heavy mesh construction.
99.wh: Traditional methods (finite element or finite difference) require meshing the domain, often with extreme refinement near geometric features. Grid-free Monte Carlo methods (random walk techniques) adapt to any geometry but lose accuracy fast, especially near boundaries. Neither approach is ideal: finite element is slow and meshing-heavy; Monte Carlo is grid-free but high-variance and slow to converge.
99.ap: Walk on Decomposed Subdomains combines both approaches. The domain is split into simple, regular pieces. Within each piece, Monte Carlo estimates local solutions (Poisson kernels) where random walks are short and variance is controlled. These local solutions are assembled into a sparse global system solved deterministically, replacing the need to simulate random walks across the whole domain.
99.ww: Decomposition makes Monte Carlo estimates stable: short walks mean low variance. The deterministic global solve then uses these local operators as building blocks, trading the stochastic variance of long walks for a fixed, resolution-dependent discretization error. The local estimates are reusable across different boundary conditions, further amortizing cost.
99.po: The method combines the geometric flexibility and parallelism of Monte Carlo with the stability of deterministic solves. It naturally handles arbitrary and evolving geometry without meshing, adapts computational effort to geometry complexity, and provides stable, reusable solution operators for repeated problems.

100.bp: Camera lenses today are not just optical systems—they're part of an end-to-end pipeline: optics capture light, then software reconstructs and enhances the image. Modern design should optimize the optics specifically for the downstream software, not for traditional goals like flat focus or low aberration. This needs better mathematical tools.
100.wh: Optimizing optics jointly with software means the designer must choose from thousands of optical parameters to minimize a single number (image quality or reconstruction loss). The Jacobian matrix (how each parameter affects the result) becomes rank-deficient: there are many more parameters than constraints, so standard least-squares methods like Levenberg-Marquardt fail with numerical instability.
100.ap: The paper introduces generalized transverse ray aberrations (GTRA), a generalization of classical spot-radius optimization. Instead of working with a single scalar loss, GTRA lifts scalar task-driven losses into high-dimensional ray-level residuals. This creates many more constraints, filling out the Jacobian matrix and making it invertible and well-behaved for Levenberg-Marquardt solvers.
100.ww: Classical optical design used ray aberrations (deviations per ray) to drive optimization—this gives many constraints per design. Task-driven end-to-end design uses one scalar loss—too few constraints. GTRA bridges the gap by decomposing the scalar loss back into per-ray residuals, which restores the constraint-rich structure that makes robust solvers work.
100.po: The method decisively outperforms first-order optimizers on over 100 design instances for end-to-end image restoration, including smartphone telephoto lenses, microscope objectives, and cameras. It brings the robustness of traditional optical design to the flexibility of end-to-end pipelines, making joint optimization practical.

101.bp: Animated characters in VR need to move and respond convincingly to what you're doing. A simple script that follows waypoints is rigid and unnatural. If you're hiding and the character is seeking, it should move like someone searching, not like a robot. Large language models trained on human behavior might encode this intuition.
101.wh: Agents need to generate navigation decisions that match their role in a narrative (seeker vs. hider), respond to dynamic changes in the scene or user behavior, and move in spatially consistent ways—all in real time in an immersive environment. Language models excel at reasoning but don't inherently understand spatial layout or embodied physics.
101.ap: The system feeds multimodal inputs to a large language model: scene information (geometry, room layout), user state (location, actions), and a high-level role instruction (seeker, guard, etc.). The model outputs navigation decisions and stylized planning paths. These are then executed by the virtual agent in the immersive environment.
101.ww: Modern multimodal language models integrate vision, text, and reasoning, so they can understand scene context and role constraints jointly. By grounding language instructions in spatial information, the model can reason about the character's intentions and how to move in ways that express that role.
101.po: The approach enables virtual agents to behave consistently with narrative roles and respond to dynamic actions. In examples like hide-and-seek, agents reason about the user's possible intentions given the role and the scene, generating movement behaviors that feel intentional rather than scripted.

102.bp: Creating animated characters for games and film is expensive: you model the shape, then rig it with a skeleton and weights that dictate how the surface deforms as joints move. Generative models can create static 3D shapes from images, but automatically rigging them (auto-rigging) is brittle and often produces skeletons that don't match the geometry.
102.wh: The skeleton and skin weights are invisible in the rendered image, so it's hard to predict them from vision alone. The topology of the skeleton (which joints connect) must match the topology of the shape's parts. Topology is a discrete global property; local image cues don't constrain it well. Existing systems predict rigs after generating geometry, losing geometric coherence.
102.ap: AniGen represents shape, skeleton, and skin weights as three fields (S3 Fields) defined over the same spatial domain. It treats them as mutually consistent: the skeleton should trace symmetry axes, and skin weights should distribute influence smoothly. A flow-matching generative model first synthesizes a sparse structural scaffold (rough skeleton and shape), then fills in dense geometry and articulation in a learned latent space.
102.ww: Representing all three as fields over the same space forces geometric coherence. The model learns that bone predictions are ambiguous at Voronoi boundaries (edges where multiple surface regions equidistant), so it uses a confidence-decaying skeleton field to handle uncertainty. Decoupling skin weights from specific joint counts allows one network to predict rigs of arbitrary complexity.
102.po: AniGen directly generates animate-ready 3D assets from a single image. It substantially outperforms state-of-the-art systems by producing topologically consistent skeletons and skin weights that match the generated geometry, eliminating the brittleness of post-hoc auto-rigging.

103.bp: Professional facial capture (scanning faces to build digital copies for rendering) requires expensive studio setups with precise lighting. Smartphone cameras in the wild have unpredictable, uncontrolled illumination. We want studio-quality results from casual videos, which means disentangling what the face looks like from how the lighting happened to fall on it.
103.wh: Inverse rendering—solving for surface reflectance given an image—is ill-posed when illumination is unknown. The same pixel could be bright because the surface is shiny or because the light was strong. Many combinations of reflectance and lighting explain the image equally well, so optimization gets stuck.
103.ap: Instead of purely solving for reflectance, the method trains a powerful neural "delighting" network as a prior. It learns to estimate per-pixel illumination from the input video. Training combines two sources: the OLAT dataset (same face lit from different directions) and Light Stage scans (studio gold-standard captures). Dataset Latent Modulation (DLM) fuses these heterogeneous sources by conditioning the network on learnable source-aware tokens.
103.ww: A learned delighting prior constrains the otherwise ill-posed inverse problem. The network learns which variations are reliable (surface properties) and which are artifacts of lighting from the training data. By training on both casual and studio data with source-aware conditioning, the model learns universal delighting principles rather than overfitting to one data source.
103.po: The approach enables simple, automatic appearance capture from casual smartphone video, outperforming prior methods significantly. The authors transform the multi-view NeRSemble dataset into NeRSemble-Scan, a large-scale collection of 4K-resolution relightable facial scans, and open-source both the model and dataset to democratize high-end facial capture.

104.bp: A cage is a low-polygon surface that wraps tightly around a more detailed shape. It serves as a simple proxy for rigging (animating by moving cage vertices), level-of-detail rendering, and deformation. A good cage is simple (few faces) and tight (stays close to the original shape). But simplicity and tightness fight each other.
104.wh: Aggressive simplification makes the cage diverge from the shape. Tight cages stay complex. The tradeoff is hard to navigate manually. Furthermore, simplification algorithms can create degenerate triangles (zero area) or flipped normals (facing inward), breaking geometric validity.
104.ap: PR-Cage uses nested optimization: an outer layer that guides simplification via a thickness parameter tau (defining how far the cage can stray from the original), and an inner iteration using Quadric Error Metric (QEM) with linear inequality constraints to suppress degeneracy and normal flips. The key insight is progressively relaxing tau on a schedule, which allows the algorithm to find the optimal balance between simplicity and tightness.
104.ww: Gradually relaxing the feasibility region (increasing tau) first forces a tight cage, then permits looser approximations as simplification proceeds. This guides the optimization toward good tradeoffs. Inequality constraints prevent invalid triangle configurations—the algorithm won't accept a solution with flipped normals or degenerate geometry.
104.po: PR-Cage consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving extreme simplification while maintaining high geometric fidelity. Its utility is demonstrated in downstream applications where tight cages are essential, and it relies only on simple edge operations (collapses and flips), ensuring high computational efficiency and robustness.

105.bp: When you design a character, build a video-game world, or create special effects for a film, you need 3D shapes made from triangles—the most universal building block in computer graphics. Today, most of these shapes are sculpted by hand or generated sequentially, one piece at a time, which is slow and prone to mistakes because early errors cascade through the entire process.
105.wh: The team splits the problem into two independent tasks that can happen in parallel. First, they use a diffusion model—a process that gradually refines noise into a clean image—to generate the vertex positions (the corner points of all the triangles). They organize these vertices as an octree, which is a hierarchical 3D grid that lets them work coarse to fine, like sketching with broad strokes then adding detail. Second, they tackle the harder problem: figuring out which vertices connect to form faces (the actual triangles). They invented something called Space-time Interval, an extension of a prior concept called Spacetime Distance, that encodes all the connectivity information into a smooth, continuous embedding per vertex. Then another diffusion model reconstructs those embeddings to recover the final shape.
105.ww: Splitting vertex generation from connectivity generation avoids the bottleneck: vertices can be created efficiently without worrying about topology, and then topology can be derived globally rather than point-by-point. The diffusion approach inherently captures global structure because it refines the entire shape at once, and diffusion models are proven to be good at learning structure from data. The continuous embeddings from Space-time Interval allow complex, non-obvious topology—including non-standard configurations where surfaces fold in on themselves—to be recovered smoothly and globally.
105.po: The method outperforms hand-crafted, sequential approaches on standard datasets, and blind studies from 3D practitioners show strong preference for the results. It handles arbitrarily complex topology and scales to real-world scenarios like generating shapes from photographs, making it practical for production film, gaming, and interactive applications.

106.bp: When engineers design structures like buildings, bridges, or aircraft, they need to simulate how the thing vibrates and moves when disturbed. This vibrational analysis is critical for safety and performance, but for large, complex structures, the math becomes so expensive that it can take days to compute on supercomputers.
106.wh: The full problem is too large to solve in one go. Standard approaches divide the structure into smaller chunks (substructures) and solve each one independently, then stitch the results together. But the quality of the results depends on having a good basis—a set of mathematical building blocks—that captures all the important vibrational modes. When you use just the natural vibrations from each individual substructure, you don't get enough diversity to represent the full structure's behavior accurately, so you need many more modes than should theoretically be necessary.
106.ap: Instead of using vibration modes from just one partition of the structure, the researchers use modes from multiple overlapping partitions—like dividing a bridge into chunks in different ways and mining vibrations from each way separately. This gives a richer set of building blocks. They further speed things up by approximating the interfaces between chunks (the boundaries where pieces touch) using low-frequency signals derived from those modes, rather than keeping the full expensive representation at every interface.
106.ww: Overlapping partitions expose more of the structure's natural patterns; each partition captures different aspects of how the thing wants to move. Using modes from many different partitions is like getting suggestions from many different people—you get a more complete picture. The low-frequency approximation at interfaces works because most of the important information lives in the big, slow vibrations, not the tiny, fast ones, so you can throw away the fast wiggles without losing much accuracy.
106.po: The method improves accuracy by three orders of magnitude compared to standard Component Mode Synthesis, meaning you get the same answer using vastly fewer mathematical degrees of freedom. It also scales better on distributed supercomputers—communication and memory usage both improve—making large-scale simulations for film effects and industrial design far more practical.

107.bp: A bar chart showing sales numbers is precise but forgettable. A pictorial chart—one where bars are replaced by stacks of little coins or houses or people—is fun to look at and memorable. The challenge is to automate this transformation: take a boring statistical chart and turn it into an artistically compelling visual story while keeping the numbers accurate.
107.wh: You want two things at once, and they pull in opposite directions. You want artistic flair and visual interest—textures, shapes, thematic imagery—but you also want the chart to faithfully represent the underlying data. A system that blindly stylizes images might make things beautiful but wrong. You need a system that understands what the chart means (the statistics) and also respects the abstract structure (the grid, the axes, the proportions) while layering on artistic expression.
107.ap: The researchers frame this as two parallel control signals guiding a generative model. One signal is a text prompt—a description of the visual or semantic intent, like "underwater theme" or "ancient Rome." The other signal is the original statistical chart itself, which provides the structure: "this bar is 30% of the total, arranged vertically." They use a Diffusion Transformer (a neural network trained to gradually refine images) and inject two mechanisms to keep it honest: structural alignment, which anchors the output's spatial layout to the input chart, and semantic alignment, which borrows textures and artistic details from reference images to fill in the aesthetic layer.
107.ww: By separating structure from aesthetics as two independent controls, the model can learn them independently and then fuse them. The structural alignment acts as a "fence" preventing the artistic layers from distorting the data representation. The semantic alignment lets you borrow real, coherent visual styles rather than hallucinating them, because the model is conditioned on references that have the textures you want. Diffusion models naturally excel at composing multiple conditions into a coherent image.
107.po: The system produces pictorial charts that are both artistically compelling and mathematically faithful across diverse visual channels—length, area, angle, position—and semantic domains. Quantitative tests and user studies show it outperforms simpler approaches like stylization or image editing, enabling visual storytelling that actually respects the underlying data.

108.bp: When you scan a real object with depth sensors or photogrammetry, or when a neural network predicts a 3D shape from an image, you get a continuous mathematical surface representation called a signed distance function. But some shapes—statues with overhangs, cloth with folds, hollow objects—can't be cleanly represented this way because the math breaks down at spots where topology is weird. You need a different representation that can handle any topology: unsigned distance functions.
108.wh: Unsigned distance functions (the distance from any point to the nearest surface, without caring about inside vs. outside) can represent any topology, including non-manifold shapes where surfaces fold back on themselves. But here's the catch: the standard tool for extracting a triangle mesh from these functions—Dual Contouring, which works brilliantly for signed distance—relies on detecting sign changes to figure out where the surface is. Without the sign, you lose that signal, and active-cube detection becomes unreliable. Also, in non-manifold regions, even detecting where to put triangle vertices becomes ambiguous.
108.ap: The researchers adapt Dual Contouring to work on unsigned distances, calling it DCx. Instead of asking "did the sign flip?", they use optimization to decide which voxel blocks (small 2×2×2 cubes) are active. Then, crucially, they operate on expanded cubes—groups of eight voxels—and use a lookup table mapping each possible local voxel configuration to a set of connectivity patterns (which vertices connect to which). This replaces hand-coded logic with template-based extraction: given a configuration, you already know which triangles to place and how they connect.
108.ww: Optimization-based activation works because unsigned distance can still be queried at every point; you just need to decide activity differently. The lookup table approach is powerful because it encodes non-manifold connectivity rules directly. By working on expanded cubes rather than individual voxels, the method has enough local context to make the right connectivity choices, avoiding the failure modes of standard Dual Contouring on unsigned distance.
108.po: DCx successfully extracts both manifold and non-manifold surface meshes from neural unsigned distance functions, which are increasingly common in neural 3D reconstruction. The method is simple, easy to implement, and handles edge cases that broke prior work, making it practical for generative 3D and reconstruction pipelines.

109.bp: In film and games, dressing a character in clothing is tedious. A designer places each garment by hand, adjusting folds and collisions. The dream is to build a library of real clothing and characters, then automatically dress any character in any garment, even if they're wildly different shapes (a human in a robot's outfit, a cartoon character in historical armor). This would unlock massive asset reuse.
109.wh: Garments and characters rarely come from the same pipeline; they have different underlying structures (skeletons), different body shapes, different numbers of vertices, and different geometric scales. Standard correspondence methods—figuring out which point on the garment touches which point on the body—assume dense point-to-point alignment, which breaks when you're trying to match a tight shirt designed for one body to a completely different body with different proportions. You also need the clothing to drape realistically under gravity, not just snap into place.
109.ap: The key insight is to use a universal intermediate form: SMPL, a standard parametric human body model. They break the problem into two stages. First, align the garment to SMPL using a geometry-driven method that understands shape. Second, align SMPL to the target character (human, robot, cartoon) using a diffusion model that leverages both rich visual features from multiple camera angles and a pretrained 2D vision model that understands human form, even across stylization. Once they have correspondences, they register SMPL's displacement surface to the garment, then smoothly transition the garment through SMPL to the target body, using physics simulation to make it drape naturally.
109.ww: SMPL acts as a Rosetta Stone: every garment learns to align to it, and every character learns to align to it, so transitively they can all align to each other. Using a diffusion model for the second stage is smart because it's naturally good at understanding spatial correspondence under large pose and shape changes. The physics simulation ensures the garment doesn't pass through bodies or fold unnaturally; it finds the equilibrium state under gravity.
